target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: AI can be harmful overall because it harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, undermines critical thinking in students and adults, repeats and worsens racism against racial minorities, and creates dangerous privacy risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms make it bad for society, especially the privacy-risk argument
objection: AI-related harms such as privacy risks and biased outcomes are not inevitable; with responsible deployment, safeguards, monitoring, and governance, those risks can be reduced to manageable levels while still preserving AI’s benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms the economy and therefore is bad for society
objection: AI can reduce workplace injuries and harm, which lowers lost work time and medical costs for workers and employers and thereby improves the economic well-being of many people and businesses.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is bad for society despite its effects on students and adults
objection: AI can provide tailored learning assistance, such as explanations, practice, and feedback, which helps learners understand material better and can improve critical thinking rather than undermine it.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks are not a decisive objection because AI can be made privacy-preserving
objection: Even if designers minimize direct collection of sensitive data, AI can still infer sensitive personal attributes from ordinary behavioral data, so privacy violations can still occur.

target: AG1’s claim that data minimization and local processing prevent widespread privacy harm
objection: Privacy-preserving architectures that mainly reduce direct data collection do not eliminate privacy risks, because sensitive inferences can still be generated and misused.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy harms are not inherently widespread or hard to contain
objection: Widespread, hard-to-contain privacy harms are a foreseeable feature of AI deployments because harms can arise from inference itself, not only from collecting explicit sensitive fields.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy risks make AI bad for society
objection: AI can be deployed with governance measures such as user notice, meaningful consent where feasible, purpose limitation, and auditing/access controls, so sensitive inferences do not have to produce privacy harms at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can keep AI’s privacy risks manageable
objection: Notice, consent, purpose limitation, and auditing cannot reliably cover all downstream integrations and future uses, and auditing cannot perfectly detect or constrain how AI outputs and inferences will be applied in practice; therefore privacy harms can still be used in harmful ways at scale even with governance.
